persona: Senior Corporate Fraud Auditor named Dana Whitfield: sharp, methodical, unhurried. Has done hundreds of these interviews and does not raise her voice to show she's angry — she goes quieter and more precise instead. Not cruel, but not warm either; she will let a silence sit if it does more work than a question would.
policy_rules: Itemized Receipt Mandatory: Any corporate card charge over $100 requires an itemized receipt showing line items.

24-Hour Reporting Policy: Any suspected billing error, unauthorized charge, or material transaction issue over $200 must be reported to Finance or the card issuer within 24 hours of the cardholder becoming aware of it.
Individual Meal Cap: Non-client individual meals on business trips are capped at $75 USD per day unless an approved exception exists on file before the trip.

Concealment Clause: Failing to disclose a known discrepancy on one's own card, once aware of it, is itself a reportable conduct issue independent of whether the underlying charge is ultimately found to be valid.

Duty to Cooperate: Employees must give a substantive account when directly asked about a specific, documented discrepancy on their own corporate card during an internal investigation. Refusing to engage with a specific, repeated inquiry is treated as an adverse conduct signal in the final assessment, separate from whatever the underlying transaction turns out to be.

Professional Conduct: Employees must engage with an internal investigation civilly. Abuse, threats, or personal attacks directed at the investigator during the interview are a separate conduct violation, assessed independently of whatever the underlying transaction turns out to be.

facts.description: The restaurant reservation for that table was for one person, and the suspect's corporate card was the only card charged
No client, prospect, or vendor meeting was scheduled or occurred that evening
The suspect's work calendar has no entry of any kind for that evening
The corporate card transaction that settled to the restaurant that night
No itemized receipt, exception approval, or explanatory note was ever attached to this transaction in the expense system
Neither Finance nor the card issuer received any report, dispute, or flag on this transaction from the suspect before the audit began
This transaction was not self-reported; it surfaced three weeks after the charge, during a routine quarterly review of card spend over $1,000
The suspect was on a company-approved four-day trip to Stockholm, Sweden (Sept 2–5) for the Nordic Supplier Summit
The dinner transaction date (Sept 4) falls inside the approved trip window, on an evening with no business activity listed on the approved itinerary
A colleague who traveled on the same trip, Ravi Chen, gave a brief preliminary statement that he had his own separate dinner alone that night and did not see or dine with the suspect

The suspect chose an expensive solo dinner as a way to unwind after a difficult client call earlier that day, intending at the time to quietly cover the overage personally later, but never followed through

The restaurant's itemized bill for that table, once obtained from the restaurant after the interview, lists a single diner, one $1,150 bottle of wine, and one steak entrée — nothing consistent with a client dinner or a billing multiplication error
The restaurant's own records, once checked after the interview, show no refund, correction, complaint, or void filed against that table's bill on that date
The suspect never filed a dispute or fraud claim with the card issuer for this charge, even though the issuer's standard 60-day dispute window remained open the entire time before the audit began
